blocks.text: PROPHET IN THE DAYS OF JOTHAM, AHAZ AND HEZEKIAH, KINGS OF JUDAH · TWO KINGDOMS
Micah. His word that Zion would be ploughed was quoted by the elders in Jeremiah's defence, in the days of Jehoiakim.
“The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite ... which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.”
“The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite ... which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.” Micah 1:1
Against prophets who cry “Peace” for food, he says, “But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD”. Micah 3:5–8
He spoke “to all the people of Judah”, as the elders remembered. Jeremiah 26:18
“Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death?”
The word in its main themes
“Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps”
The powerful who devour the poor
“They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity”
“Thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace”
“nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more”
“But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel”
“He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
Who is a God like thee
“Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity”
To whom the word was spoken
“Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard”
“O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast”
TO THE HEADS OF JACOB AND PRINCES OF ISRAEL
“Hear, I pray you, O heads of Jacob, and ye princes of the house of Israel; Is it not for you to know judgment?”
“Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field”
“But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah”
1 Samaria and Judah judged; a remnant gathered Micah 1:1–2:13
2 Against the rulers and the prophets; Zion ploughed Micah 3:1–12
3 The mountain of the LORD; the ruler from Bethlehem Micah 4:1–5:15
4 The LORD's controversy; who is a God like thee Micah 6:1–7:20
WHERE THE NEW TESTAMENT QUOTES IT · 2
Each band joins a chapter of Micah to the New Testament book quoting it (one book).
Who stood with him, and against him
Certain of the elders of the land
Scripture does not record Micah's death. In the reign of Jehoiakim his words were still quoted in Jerusalem. Jeremiah 26:1 Jeremiah 26:17–19

Pseudo-Epiphanius makes Micah an Ephraimite and says that “for his inauspicious prophecy” he was killed by order of Ahab, thrown from a precipice, and buried at Morathi. The Jewish Encyclopedia says he is confounding Micah with Micaiah son of Imlah, who prophesied to Ahab; Micah's own heading names Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Micah 1:1 1 Kings 22:8–28 [20] Who says so: The pseudo-Epiphanian Lives of the Prophets, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904), date of the Lives not given in the source read
J. D. Michaelis, Gesenius and others, as listed by J. A. Alexander (1846); Alexander himself leans this way
Alexander: the passage's close tie to its context in Micah “somewhat favours the conclusion that Isaiah took the text or theme of his prediction from the younger though contemporary prophet”.[2]
Vitringa, Lowth and others, as listed by Alexander (1846)
Alexander lists this as one of five views held in his day.[2]
Both took it from an older oracle
Koppe, Rosenmüller, De Wette and others, as listed by Alexander (1846); G. A. Smith (1896) keeps it open

Alexander himself thinks the small differences may be “best explained” by both prophets using “a traditional prediction current among the people” or receiving it directly from the Holy Spirit. G. A. Smith thinks Micah has the more original form.[2][6]
Added later to one or both books
B. Stade, H. Hackmann and T. K. Cheyne, as reported by G. A. Smith (1896)

Smith reports the view that the oracle was inserted by later editors in both Micah and Isaiah. He himself finds it “improbable that the same post-exilic insertion should find its way into two separate books”.[6]
Micah 1 Micah 2 Micah 3 Micah 4 Micah 5 Micah 6 Micah 7 Jeremiah 26 Matthew 2
Micah's father is not named, and Scripture does not say how he died.
Micah 1:1 calls him “the Morasthite”; Scripture does not say more about his town.
Scripture records no meeting between Micah and Isaiah, though both spoke in Hezekiah's days.
